children: A wide morning view of a Kachchh village: round huts and thorn trees on a flat horizon, long blue-and-red cloths drying on the ground, a printer stirring a vat. In front, the reader raises a hand and asks how indigo turns blue.
The printer and the reader hold a printed cloth between them and lower it together into a vat set in the ground. A clock marks ten to fifteen minutes.

Seen through a big lens inside the vat: rod-shaped bacteria cling to dark grains of indigo beside cotton fibres, and on the other side of an arrow the grains are gone, dissolved. The reader peers in, mouth open.
Hands lift the cloth out of the vat. It drips bright green at the bottom and has turned blue from the top down, as pairs of oxygen atoms drift in from the air. The reader throws up both hands.
Four cloths hang on a line, each a deeper blue than the last, tagged one to four. The reader counts them off on their fingers.
Payoff: by a stream, the printer and the reader hold up the finished ajrakh between them, deep blue with red stars and borders. Water drips from it clear, and the blue stays.
